1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 47-year-old man with a chief complaint of "cough and chest tightness for more than 1 month." One month before admission, he developed cough and chest tightness without an obvious trigger, mainly dry cough, without fever, night sweats, chest pain, dyspnea, or other discomfort. During hospitalization at Hospital A, he had fever, with a maximum temperature of 37.5℃. Initial CBC showed EOS% 7.8% and eosinophil count 0.6*10^9. Chest CT showed multiple tiny nodules in the right lung and right-sided inflammatory lesions. He was treated with levofloxacin + cefonicid for 10 days. Repeat chest CT showed progression of the inflammation compared with before, and right pleural effusion appeared. Pleural fluid results showed monocyte-predominant exudative fluid, with normal ADA. Treatment was adjusted to moxifloxacin for anti-infective therapy for 4 days, but symptoms did not improve significantly. The patient was then hospitalized at Hospital B for further treatment. Repeat evaluation of the pleural effusion showed no malignant tumor cells on pleural fluid exfoliative cytology, and smear showed a large number of lymphocytes and eosinophils. Bone marrow aspiration was completed, suggesting increased eosinophil proportion. CBC showed EOS% 20% and eosinophil count 1.74*10^9. Pulmonary eosinophilia was considered. He was given loratadine for antiallergic treatment and moxifloxacin for anti-infective therapy, but his symptoms still did not improve. He was transferred to our hospital for further treatment. The patient has a past history of chronic hepatitis B and has been treated with entecavir for 2 years. He also has a history of allergic rhinitis for more than 20 years, with mildly elevated eosinophils at baseline; no definite allergen has been identified. He works as a pharmacist and denies occupational exposure to toxic or harmful substances. Physical examination: vital signs stable, conscious and alert, breathing unlabored, oxygen saturation 99%. No skin rash or ecchymoses; no superficial lymphadenopathy palpable. No cyanosis of the lips. The thorax was symmetric; tactile fremitus was slightly decreased in the right lower lung; no pleural friction fremitus was detected; the left lung was resonant to percussion; dullness to percussion was present in the right lower lung; breath sounds were decreased in the right lower lung; no dry or wet rales were heard. Heart rhythm was regular, with no pathologic murmurs. No obvious abnormalities were found on cardiac, abdominal, or neurologic examination, and there was no edema in either lower extremity.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Correlate with imaging: primary lesion with expansile growth, heterogeneous central enhancement, and an indistinct interface with the vascular wall
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient presented with cough and chest tightness, with a disease course of more than 1 month. Anti-infective and anti-allergic treatments were both ineffective. Although pulmonary artery CTA suggested "embolism" in the main trunk of the right pulmonary artery, the onset was insidious with slow progression, without typical acute pulmonary embolism-like sudden chest pain and dyspnea, and there was no definite deep venous thrombosis of the lower extremities or common thrombotic risk factors. Therefore, further detailed imaging evaluation of the lesion morphology is needed. The key is to determine whether the lesion is a simple thrombus or an intraluminal space-occupying lesion arising from the pulmonary artery. Imaging findings of a main trunk lesion, expansile growth, heterogeneous central enhancement, and an indistinct boundary with the vessel wall are more supportive of a pulmonary artery tumor rather than an ordinary thrombus. The clinical purpose of this examination is to define the location and extent of the lesion and its relationship to the vessel wall, distinguish thrombus from tumor, assess whether the main pulmonary artery and distal branches are involved, and provide a basis for subsequent decisions regarding surgery, the extent of surgical resection, and risk assessment.

With the patient’s chest tightness and cough continuing to progress, anti-infective treatment ineffective, and routine screening for infection, parasites, and rheumatologic/immunologic disease all lacking supportive evidence, while pulmonary artery CTA only suggested “embolism,” PET-CT was used to further determine whether the lesion was a metabolically inactive thrombus or an intraluminal malignant lesion of the pulmonary artery with tumor biological activity. Focal hypermetabolism suggests a significantly increased likelihood of tumor and helps revise the original diagnosis of pulmonary embolism toward pulmonary artery sarcoma. On the other hand, PET-CT can also assess whether there are other hypermetabolic foci throughout the body, helping determine whether this is a primary pulmonary artery lesion or pulmonary artery involvement by metastasis/another primary tumor, thereby completing staging and guiding surgery and subsequent chemotherapy selection.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Direct pulmonary artery pressure measurement after stripping: 45/11(21) mmHg
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The lesion is located in the main trunk of the right pulmonary artery. Clinically, there is chest tightness, and imaging suggests involvement of the central great vessels. It is necessary to assess pulmonary artery outflow tract obstruction caused by the lesion and its hemodynamic impact. Direct pulmonary artery pressure measurement can objectively reflect the level of pulmonary artery pressure and the immediate hemodynamic status after surgical relief of the obstruction, determine the severity of the tumor's burden on the pulmonary circulation, and also help compare it with pulmonary hypertension after simple chronic thromboembolism. This examination is very important in the perioperative period: on the one hand, it is used to assess disease severity and surgical benefit; on the other hand, it is used intraoperatively and postoperatively to determine whether endarterectomy was adequate and whether residual obstruction remains significant, and to provide a basis for postoperative monitoring, anticoagulation, and subsequent comprehensive treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Postoperative pathology suggested a malignant spindle cell tumor with necrosis of the "pulmonary artery thrombus"
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although the patient was initially considered to have pulmonary embolism, the clinical course was not consistent with a typical acute thrombus, and imaging had already suggested the possibility of an intraluminal space-occupying lesion; the final diagnosis still had to rely on histopathology. Postoperative pathology is the gold standard for resolving the core question of “true thrombus versus tumor embolism/primary pulmonary artery tumor.” Pathology revealed a malignant spindle cell tumor with necrosis, directly refuting the explanation of simple thromboembolic pulmonary embolism and confirming that the lesion is a malignant mesenchymal tumor. This examination is used not only for definitive diagnosis, but also to determine whether subsequent treatment should follow a sarcoma pathway, including whether adjuvant chemotherapy should be given, how prognosis should be assessed, and whether further molecular pathologic subtyping is needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immunohistochemistry: Vimentin(+), CD56(+), CD99(+), MDM-2(+), CDK4(focally weak +), Ki67(approximately 30%+ in hotspot areas), SMA(-), MyoD1(-), AE1/AE3(-), Desmin(-), Myogenin(-), S-100(-), CD34(-), CD31(-), Factor 8(-), BCL-2(-), HHV-8(-), ALK-1(-)
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although the postoperative pathology had already indicated a malignant spindle cell tumor, the differential diagnosis of spindle cell tumors is broad, including smooth muscle origin, skeletal muscle origin, epithelial origin, neurogenic origin, vascular origin, and other undifferentiated sarcomas; therefore, further immunohistochemistry was required to clarify the direction of differentiation and exclude important differential diagnoses. In conjunction with the immunophenotype in this case, Vimentin positivity supports a mesenchymal origin; MDM2 and CDK4 expression are clues associated with pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma, whereas negative SMA, Desmin, MyoD1, and Myogenin do not support smooth muscle or skeletal muscle differentiation; negative AE1/AE3 does not support carcinoma; negative S-100 does not support neurogenic origin; and negative CD31, CD34, and Factor8 do not support a vascular endothelial origin. Ki67 of approximately 30% suggests active proliferation and is helpful in assessing the degree of malignancy. This examination directly serves pathologic classification, exclusion of differential diagnoses, and guidance of subsequent chemotherapy strategy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: STAB2 FISH test result (FISH20-1332): MDM2 gene distribution: clustered distribution; MDM2 gene test result: (+)
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In the diagnosis of a primary malignant spindle cell tumor of the pulmonary artery, molecular pathology helps increase diagnostic confidence, especially when the morphologic features and immunohistochemistry suggest an undifferentiated sarcoma but further distinction from other spindle cell tumors is still required. The patient's lesion was located in the main pulmonary artery; imaging and PET-CT had already suggested a neoplastic lesion, and the postoperative pathology and immunohistochemistry supported a sarcoma. At this point, STAB2/MDM2-related FISH testing was performed to look for evidence of molecular abnormalities commonly seen in pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma. MDM2 positivity can serve as important molecular evidence supporting primary pulmonary artery sarcoma, especially the intimal sarcoma lineage, further strengthening the final diagnosis, reducing confusion with bland thrombus, sarcomas from other origins, or metastatic tumors, and it is of important value for subsequent pathologic grading, prognostic assessment, and formulation of a postoperative chemotherapy regimen.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: The patient is a middle-aged man with no prior risk factors for thrombosis and no deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremities. The onset was insidious with slow progression, without sudden dyspnea, chest pain, or other manifestations, unlike acute thrombotic pulmonary embolism. In conjunction with imaging findings: a main pulmonary artery lesion, expansile growth, heterogeneous central enhancement, indistinct demarcation from the vessel wall, and focal hypermetabolism on PET-CT. After consultation with cardiac surgery, surgical indications were considered present. After contraindications were excluded, pulmonary artery intraluminal mass resection was performed under general anesthesia and cardiopulmonary bypass. Intraoperatively: complete endarterectomy of the pulmonary artery was performed starting to the right pulmonary artery and extending to the segmental vessel level. After endarterectomy, direct pulmonary artery pressure measurement was 45/11(21) mmHg. Postoperative pathology indicated a malignant spindle cell tumor with necrosis in the "pulmonary artery thrombus." Immunohistochemistry: Vimentin(+), CD56(+), CD99(+), MDM-2(+), CDK4(focally +), Ki67(approximately 30%+ in hot spots), SMA(-), MyoD1(-), AE1/AE3(-), Desmin(-), Myogenin(-), S-100(-), CD34(-), CD31(-), Factor8(-), BCL-2(-), HHV-8, ALK-1(-). STAB2 FISH result (FISH20-1332): MDM2 gene distribution pattern: clustered distribution. MDM2 gene test result: (+).
